The (CH3)2NH2CuCl3 crystals were grown using a slow evaporation method with different solvents, temperatures, and degrees of supersaturation.
Alcohol was found to be the best solvent for growing the (CH3)2NH2CuCl3 crystals, producing the largest crystals up to 12x7x4 mm in size.
The optimal growth temperature was around 35°C, which produced high-quality crystals.
The degree of supersaturation of the solution was important, with a ratio of 1 mmol raw materials to 10 ml solvent producing the best quality crystals.
The (CH3)2NH2CuCl3 crystals had a monoclinic structure (space group I2/a) with lattice parameters a = 11.97 Å, b = 8.6258 Å, c = 14.34 Å, and β = 97.47°.
Magnetic susceptibility measurements showed a Curie-like behavior with no magnetic transition down to 2 K.
Specific heat measurements revealed the low-field antiferromagnetic ordering, the field-induced spin gapped state, and the field-induced magnetic ordering.
The crystal shape and quality were strongly dependent on the growth temperature, with higher quality crystals obtained at 35°C.
The ability to grow high-quality crystals was found to strongly depend on the structural similarity between the solute and the solvent.
The problem of the crystals deliquescing in air was solved through a recrystallization process.
The largest crystal obtained was 12x7x4 mm in size, grown from a 100 ml alcohol solution containing 15 mmol each of CuCl2·2H2O and (CH3)2NH2Cl.
Methanol was not a suitable solvent for growing high-quality (CH3)2NH2CuCl3 crystals.
The crystals grown at 20°C in water had a flat, irregular shape and poor quality.
The crystals grown at 35°C in alcohol had a typical size of 3-7 mm x 2-3 mm x 2-4 mm and high quality.
The crystals grown at 20°C in alcohol had considerably large sizes but poor quality.
